The nocturnal, flightless Kakapo of New Zealand exhibits a suite of life-history traits profoundly shaped by its island environment and extreme longevity. Captive-rearing programs have documented that hatchlings emerge after an incubation period of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature that reflects the species’ unusual slow developmental pace. Newly hatched chicks weigh a mere 28.9 grams [Wwb = 28.9 grams], a neonatal mass that is remarkably low for a parrot species that will eventually attain a substantial adult size. This initial mass is supported by a large yolk reserve, and the altricial nestling depends entirely on parental provisioning during the first weeks of life. The extended incubation and low hatchling mass are consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises long-term survival over rapid offspring production, a pattern seen in other long-lived seabirds and kiwis from similar predator-free environments.

Field observations of the reproductive behaviour of the Kakapo reveal an exceptionally slow and intermittent breeding cycle, tightly coupled to the irregular mast fruiting of native trees such as the rimu. The extreme rarity of successful breeding events means that a female may only raise a handful of chicks over her entire lifetime, a stark contrast to the annual reproductive cycles of most psittacines.

The developmental trajectory from hatchling to independence in the Kakapo is notably protracted, even by the standards of large, long-lived parrots. Under the species’ typical active body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the fledging stage, defined as the age at which the chick achieves sustained flight and leaves the nest, occurs at approximately 76 days after hatching [tx = approximately 76 days after hatching]. This milestone is followed by an extended period of post-fledging care during which the mother continues to provision the chick for several more months. The pre-fledging mass for a male chick at this stage has been recorded at 1984 grams [Wwx = 1984 grams], representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass. This slow maturation is a direct consequence of a low metabolic rate and a diet of low-nutrient foods, ensuring that the chick invests heavily in structural growth before becoming fully independent.

The onset of puberty and the ability to reproduce are separated by several years in the Kakapo, a key feature of its extreme slow life history. This gap between puberty and first breeding is thought to be a strategic delay, allowing the young bird to establish a territory and build up the necessary fat reserves to support the enormous energetic demands of egg production.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in the Kakapo, a trait linked to the species’ lek breeding system. The ultimate wet weight, or the maximum adult body mass recorded for females, is approximately 1750 grams [Wwi = approximately 1750 grams], a substantial mass for any parrot. Males, which compete for display sites and must sustain a long mating season, can reach a significantly larger ultimate wet weight of 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams]. These masses are maintained on a herbivorous diet of leaves, stems, and fruits, with males sometimes doubling their weight during the breeding season before fasting. The high body mass, combined with extreme longevity and a reproductive rate limited to one to two eggs per breeding attempt [N_R_i = one to two eggs per breeding attempt] occurring infrequently [F_R_i = infrequently], means that the species has a negligible capacity for rapid population recovery, making it exceptionally vulnerable to introduced predators and habitat loss.
